utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Selimi, the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Whiting: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selimi, I just have a few final questions. With the assistance of the usher I'm going to show you some more photographs, and if they could be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If they can be placed one at a time. The first one is 3704, U008-3704.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selimi, could you look to your left, please, at the photograph. Now, looking at the photograph on the lower part of that page, could you identify who those individuals are?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm having some trouble with my earphones. Okay. Could you tell us who these three people are and when, if you recall, this photo was taken and where.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's myself, in the middle, with Sahit Jashari and Muse Jashari. Sahit Jashari is on my left in the photo. Muse Jashari is on my right side in the photo. This photo, from what I can see in the background, was taken in Likovc. I don't know exactly the time when it was taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately the time? For example, do you know the year?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be in 1999; it may be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look at the next photograph which is 3708, please. Drawing your attention to the photograph on the lower part of the page, can you identify who the individuals are in that photograph, when you think it was taken, and where.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's myself. Next to me is Daut Haradinaj and on the other side is Sylejman Selimi. This photo must have been taken in Albania during 1997.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next photograph is 3709. Can you identify the individuals in this photograph, when you think it was taken, and where. And maybe the best way to do it is do the -- identify the four people who are standing and then the person who's kneeling.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beginning from my left side is Muje Krasniqi; he's a martyr to the nation. Second is myself. The third person is Adem Jashari. The fourth standing is Xheladin Gashi and the person sitting is Hamze Jashari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us when this photograph was taken and where?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be the beginning of 1997 in Prekaz in the yard of Commander Adem Jashari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next photograph is 3721. I think we have to pull out for this one. Do you recognise the individuals in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who they are?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I see, it's Fatmir Limaj and Ismet Jashari, Kumanova.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please ask the witness to wait for the translation of the question before answering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selimi, the interpreters have asked that, if you could, wait until the translation of the question is completed before you answer the question; it will make their job easier.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next photograph is 3726. Drawing your attention on this page to the top photograph, can you identify who the individuals are in that photograph and when and where you think it was taken.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On my left side is Bashkim Jashari, then Fatmir Limaj, Sami Lustaku, myself. A few others I cannot identify very well. This picture must have been taken in the Pristina stadium in September 1999 on the day of demilitarisation and transformation of the KLA into the TMK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next photograph is 3730, and it's the lower photograph that I want to ask you about, the one on the bottom. Can you identify the individuals in that photograph and, if you know, when it was taken and where?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's myself when I was part of the KPC or TMK. You can see that from my uniform. On my left is Xhavid Haliti. On my right, if I can be right, is Fatmir Limaj. Next to him is Sylejman Selimi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when that photograph was taken and where?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. It must be the year either 2000 or 2001, given by the uniform I'm wearing. Probably we've been in some memorial rally. I don't remember exactly when because we had plenty of such ceremonies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, if you could look at paragraph 3729. And I draw your attention to the top photograph on this page. Same question: Do you -- can you recognise who's in the photograph, when it was taken and where it was taken?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where. It may be during one of the rallies which we used to hold in memory of the martyrs. It might be the same year, 2000, or 2001 because I'm wearing uniform. The people close to me are Ram Buja and Fatmir Limaj, even though the quality of the photo is very poor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Ram Buja on your right or your left in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is on my right side, but I want to stress the fact that it's of a very poor quality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this group of photographs be given a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. This group of six photographs is given the Exhibit number P248. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think there were seven photographs, just so the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you allow me to say something? Until now, I am hearing only the English version. I can't get Albanian translation so far. I didn't say this before, not to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. I will alert the usher --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could the usher please check the channel. We may have been on the wrong channel. Are you now hearing me translated to your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's sorted. And it would appear there were seven rather than six photographs in the exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selimi, just so there's no difficulty with the record, did you have any difficulty understanding my questions, even though they weren't being translated to you in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any further questions. I did want to raise one small matter with the Court, which is -- which I've raised with Defence counsel and it's with regards to the video-clip that was played yesterday. Of course there was no translation again during that clip, which was the procedure we had adopted with the testimony of Mr. Limaj. May I ask, we have prepared a transcript -- a translation of the words that were spoken on the video. I've provided it to Defence counsel, and I would just ask that for the purposes of the record that that transcript be inserted into the record at the places where the video was played. I don't think Defence counsel has a problem with that as long as they have an opportunity to check the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It appears to me it may be better if it's an exhibit rather than inserted into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. I've provided it to the Court and to Defence counsel. If it could be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If it's done that way, if there then emerges, when it's looked at, any problem with the translation, it will be much more readily corrected and dealt with. It will be received as an exhibit if that's been provided.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With the explicit provision that the registry gets a copy, yes, it will be P249, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have a copy, if that could be provided to the registrar. With that, I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Mansfield. Re-examined by Mr. Mansfield:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Selimi, I want to start by asking you some more questions about a recorded interview which is before the Tribunal at the moment, although not exhibited, where you were interviewed by the Prosecution on the 2nd of April, 2004. Do you still have the transcript in front of you? It was there yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I would ask Your Honours, please, to ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it's clear from this transcript that you had been asked to attend as a witness, and that is how you were interviewed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I, therefore, don't go through those pages, but I do want to go through the context of some of the questions you've been asked. Could you kindly turn to page 38. You have been asked questions about topics further up this page, but I'd like you to look at the bottom of this page where you're being asked about the formation of the operational zones and who was in charge of them. Do you see that? It's at the bottom of page 38.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the question in English, but maybe the answer is on the following page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct. Now, on the following page, 39, you indicate that a preferred person becomes the commander of a zone and you were asked who those persons were. Do you see those questions?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you indicate you know them all and then you name the first one as being Sylejman Selimi; that's at the bottom of page 39. And if you turn over the page to 40, you specify in turn all the zones. Now, in the context of that answer you mention, third zone down, Drenica you've mentioned at the top, is Pastrik and the commander, the first one, was Muse Jashari. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And later on, others. Just pausing for a moment. Who were the others who came later?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Pastrik Operational Zone in the beginning of the plan, of the idea, the commander of this zone was envisaged to be Muse Jashari, but it was difficult. And later continue when Muse Jashari became a chief of communications at the General Staff, Ekrem Rexha became commander of this zone. And when Ekrem Rexha assumed another duty and position at General Staff, Tahir Sinani became commander of the Pastrik zone. In other words, the Pastrik Operational Zone ended the war with three commanders, with Tahir Sinani the commander, the last one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in terms -- you started the answer there by indicating that there was a plan at the beginning. Could you clarify when -- if you can remember, when the plan was being discussed and talked about.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the developments, as for the organisation of the Drenice Operational Zone, it was necessary for it to become a zone. It was Muse Jashari who preferred to take part in the formation of this zone. He went to Malisheve because at that time there were many guerrilla units scattered in many areas, and Muse Jashari did not manage to restructure the zone. Later on it was asked from Ekrem Rexha who came from abroad, I don't know from where, he was asked to take responsibility for the organisation of this zone. In other words, the Pastrik Operational Zone faced many difficulties in its restructuring.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the many difficulties in the attempt to restructure that zone?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say "restructuring" before it being structured. Because at that time it was necessary to structure a zone, not to restructure it, because there was no previous structure. One of the most important issues was the stretch-out of the terrain. The Pastrik Operational Zone began from the Pastrik mountains, which was on the border with Albania, west from Prizren. Another problem was that there were many fightings going on and the flux of information of - correction - of population coming from endangered area to this area, either from the municipality of Suhareke or other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you give us some idea when you think the first structure of any kind could be said to have existed in Pastrik -- in the Pastrik zone?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, it was envisaged for the Pastrik Operational Zone to begin from Pastrik Mountain and to include Prizren, Rahovec, and Malisheve, and extend up to the mountains of Berisa. The other side of the Berisa Mountains could be adjoined to the Nerodime Operational Zone, because the majority of the villages there belonged to Lipjan municipality, which was intended to be part of the Nerodime zone. However, this plan did not come true and the Pastrik Operational Zone was formed as it was until the end of the war. We can say without hesitation that the structuring of the Pastrik zone began in August 1998, and the planning of the future brigades that would belong to this operational zone began without knowing the exact number of the brigades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just going -- yes, I'm asked if you would be kind enough to just keep it a little slower for the interpreters. I appreciate it's sometimes difficult. Now, just going back to the transcript on pages 40 and 41 - I don't read them all out, they're all there - you give the names of other commanders. Now, I want to just come to a section where you say -- you're talking about the level of organisation --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I -- I don't really understand why for these questions it's necessary to go through the transcript, why these questions can't simply be put to the witness rather than led through the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm going to ask, in fact, if there's no objection that this transcript -- so far it hasn't been exhibited, that in fact it's exhibited, and in that sense obviously I don't have to read it into the record. If there's no objection to that, I can do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there objection, Mr. Whiting? And secondly, does that overcome your objection? Two different objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. Well, I -- I have -- I frankly haven't considered whether this -- I have a practical problem of this transcript coming into evidence, but that's not been the practice that we've followed of prior statements of witnesses coming into evidence. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It was relied upon you in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. And the passages that I relied on were put into the record, which has been the practice. And it has not been -- with one exception, it has not been the practice to put in prior statements. In fact, it has been strictly the rule that we have not, and that's been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's you, the person calling the witness. Now, this Mr. Mansfield in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it's his witness. He's trying to put in the prior transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On which you cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. But when the Defence has cross-examined on using transcripts we have then sought to put in, there's been objection and they have not gone into evidence. So I don't -- I don't understand why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Mansfield, there is objection. I did what I could for you. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, I will continue without the transcript for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And perhaps the argument about the mission of this transcript can come later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just continue -- we're talking about the level of organisation. You were talking about it to the Prosecutor in the interview. Was the level of organisation in the various zones, as they came into being, the same for each zone?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The level of organisation was not the same and could not be the same. I will try to be helpful in order to provide you with a clear picture of the level of organisation at the war zones in that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, if you could do that, and could you remember the interpreters while you do it, please.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will do my best. The Drenica Operational Zone, which became such in May 1998, was the zone more advanced in comparison to others, both to the number of its fighters and other. The Drenice Operational Zone was Jashari's -- Adem Jashari's zone, a zone where many fightings had taken place. Therefore, it was the first zone who had the circumstances under which it could be formed. And other villages and other zones were not equal in doing the same as Drenica. The structuring of units in different positions and in different areas, Drenica was like a year ahead compared to other zones. Therefore, seeing and facing all these advantages, we concentrated in Drenica in order to create the zone. In the beginning, a command was established in the Drenica Operational Zone. All the soldiers in that area and on basis of their will, Commander Sylejman Selimi was appointed the commander of the zone, and other zones now could follow the example of Drenica, zones that were to be formed in the future. So for a relatively long period, the Drenica Operational Zone was structured and became a model for structuring other zones. It was in summer of 1998 when Drenica zone had acquired its profile, and now we had to start creating the other operational zone, the Dukagjini and Pastrik Operational Zones, and with this we began in the end of the summer. We began to apply this model to the new zones. In addition, in structuring the Drenice Operational Zone, only the borders of this zone were delineated without interfering with the borders of other operational zones. The circumstances in the terrain caused us this delay, information and establishment of other operational zones of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you a few more questions about Fatmir Limaj. You were -- you were asked about, in particular -- I think there can't be objection to me at least quoting the transcript that was quoted to you. It's -- in fact, if you need to see it it's on page 68. If you just turn to page 68. This part of the transcript has already been asked about, pages 68 and 69. Now, in particular you were asked about the fact that when he went to Malisheve he was looking for people. Can you just expand on that. Was that -- first of all, was that an official role, a military position, that he had at that time, looking for people, or what?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said and repeat, Mr. Fatmir Limaj went to his birth place to look for people. That means we hadn't enough people or structures enough to form an operational unit at that time. Something else. I want to repeat that Fatmir Limaj had no call and no role and no obligation from anybody to plan or to design an organisational or operational plan at this zone. It was a rule that was imperative -- model imperative for every soldier who was a member of KLA, at the beginning to go to his birth place and to recruit his own people. The same thing he did in Switzerland some years before. Fatmir Limaj didn't go to his birth place to visit his family but to look how he could serve his forces. With the possibility and with the circumstances existing, it was the first still unit that was formed in this region and in this region -- this vicinities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this context, another word was put to you from the transcripts, the word being "coordinating" or "coordination role." Can you just explain that for the moment?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to explain you. In the transcript it's written "coordinating person." Fatmir Limaj or neither -- no personnels could go to Malisheve without previous coordination. Without agreement with whom he would go and with what car, which vehicle he should go. Each of his actions and of his collaborators were previously agreed with his collaborators. We spoke to each other. We were in a battle. We were a well-coordinated, and we previously knew in our structure. I personally knew and I said that one of the coordinators who looked for more recruits was he. I interpret his function in this way, one of the best recruiters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having recruited people to join the KLA, would he have any further role after that?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fatmir Limaj at the beginning worked with the unit Celiku 1 at a specified place; I think it was the Malisheve region. At September 1999 -- 1998, excuse me, after all the units were concentrated in certain places, the units after Celiku, Lumi, [indiscernible], Sokoli, Luma and others, he was assigned commandment of the Ismet Jashari, Kumanova, zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just ask you about the name "Celiku." Do you know by what name he was known in the first place?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me he was known as Fatmir. As soon as he arrived from Switzerland, several persons who knew him knew him with the name Daja. And during his stay in the Malisheve zone, in Malisheve commune or municipality, in intercommunication between us he was known to me as Celiku 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you happen to know how that name came about?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I will not call it a name or a pseudonym. Celiku 1 was a communication code for us during communication between myself and him and other co-fighters. This name was given when I gave him two radios that would be used for communication between us. As I gave him two radios, I suggested that one of them should be called Celiku 1 and the other Celiku 2 so that I have the coded name in order to know where Celiku is and to be able to contact him. So I suggested this and Fatmir accepted. He was in a position not to accept if he wanted to, but he did accept it and that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn from topics that arise in the transcript to some other questions that you were asked. When did you become interior minister in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the international conference for Kosova organised at Rambouillet and Paris, the Albanian delegation had reached an internal agreement, according to which a provisional government should be formed upon return to Kosova, which task would be to surpass the problems that Kosova was going through at that time. So a delegation of the KLA, of LDK, and another party that was active at that time in Kosova known with the initials LBD drafted an agreement for the provisional government of Kosova and the mandate was given upon agreement to one of the KLA members. Those who undertook the formation of this provisional government gave this post to me. And at that time, I fulfilled the duty of the general inspector of the KLA and I was in this post until the end of the war. So in April 1999, the provisional government of Kosova was established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was in this context that you were asked by the Prosecution about being stopped and detained at a NATO checkpoint. And the suggestion was that this happened in August of 1999. Now, if it's right that it is 1999, you were then interior minister. How often were you stopped at checkpoints yourself in 1999?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but it wasn't a problem for me to be stopped at KFOR checkpoints because KFOR at that time was on a peace mission. And, therefore, for me it wasn't a problem, whether I would be stopped at checkpoints or not, despite the fact that I was a Minister of the Interior of the provisional government of Kosova. This, as I said earlier, was a routine control and to me it was not a problem. What is said in that report, most of it is not true; I don't know the reason why and I don't know who received misinformation regarding the events at that time. I was never against the rules of KFOR in Kosova and I never wanted to be against such rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we don't have the details. If there are some I'd certainly appreciate them being proffered to us. But the suggestion is that on an occasion in August 1999 you pointed a gun at British troops. Now, first of all, is there any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever been questioned on the basis that you had done that?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever been charged with any offence related to pointing a gun at British troops?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next question you may not be able to answer but please pause if you can't. If you had have pointed a gun at British troops in 1999, what would have happened?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, want to move on because the next suggestion to you was that it was your house, but then qualified, not your house. A house that was used by you was -- as a meeting place with others was searched and various items were found; they were then listed. Now, can you recall that occasion?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present when this happened?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, I wasn't present but I arrived there after KFOR had started their search.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the place itself; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This place was a private house in Pristina, property of an Albanian living in the United States, who voluntarily after the war had given this house to the KLA units to use it in Pristina. After this, as we needed a facility that we could use for our work in the government, these fighters showed us this house and told us that we could use it because they no longer had need for that house. This house is situated in Ulpiani neighbourhood in Pristina. I don't know the name of the owner. We didn't stay long in that house. We just spent some time in order to make the computer connections and to establish other things necessary for the functioning of the administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as the items found, the weapons and so on there, were they anything to do with you?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They had nothing to do with me personally because this facility had been previously used by a KLA unit, and I cannot be certain whether they left behind equipment from the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, were you ever questioned about any of this, yourself, at the time?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never invited for questioning regarding this issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move on. You were then asked about something in 2000 -- an event in 2001, in June of 2001, and being placed on a blacklist by the United States government. Now, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And some other names were put who were also apparently on this list. Were you ever told why you were on this list?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never told, despite the fact that I had made two official requests for me to be informed for the reasons of putting my name on this list, which I do not call a blacklist. But some names who were previously on this list are now partners with EU international community members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The suggestion being made, at least by the United States Government, according to the question, is that you posed a risk of threatening peace in the region. That's part of it. Now, in this period, 2001, were you engaged in any activity at all that was posing a threat to this region? The peace of the region, sorry, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this time I was member of the Kosova Protection Corps and commander of the defence academy. I was involved in training KPC members who are building peace, and they never participated in anything that could pose a threat to the peace in the region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically, were you, yourself, licensed or authorised to possess any weapons of any kind?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had an authorised weapon by KFOR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned bodyguards in answer to these questions earlier. Did you have one bodyguard or more than one?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I had two bodyguards who were also in possession of a weapon authorised by KFOR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about ammunition for the weapons?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A final question: From 1999 until the present have you been charged with any offences arising out of any of these suggestions that have been made?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's all I ask unless Your Honours have any ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mansfield. Mr. Selimi, thank you very much. That concludes the questions that are asked of you, so you're now free to go with the court officer and go back to your country. I'm sorry you had to be delayed over this last weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: She's here. It's slightly out of order. You will understand immediately I announce why she is being taken slightly out of order. Her name is Carolyn McCool and essentially she knew this defendant after the war. Carolyn McCool, please. There is an updated curriculum vitae which has been provided to everyone, and I think Your Honours have a copy of that. May I just indicate there is a further filing, annex 5, which relates to the organisation for which this witness worked at the time from Dan Everts. You will recall in fact I read some of this in the opening in November. I think there's been a mild hiatus here because -- could someone very kindly -- perhaps someone from our team could go -- there's no usher so she hasn't been actually asked for. I think she's just behind the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, without being too explicit, I think when she comes in it will be obvious she's been suffering from an illness over the recent past, and one of the reasons she has to leave is to continue the treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Whoever is behind the door is not the witness you were anticipating.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The person behind the door was expecting to be called next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, he was expecting to be called next. But -- yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I can understand why there's been a confusion. But I know Carolyn McCool is here myself because I've spoken with her myself just before we came in. I'm sorry, if we could perhaps break shortly while this is sorted out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps we will have an early break now and stretch the next two sessions as a consequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I do apologise. I'm sorry for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn now and resume at 20 minutes to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That should give you time enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Fine. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. McCool.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that's been given to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: May I thank Your Honours for the time in locating the witness and apologise to the witness for the hiatus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Mansfield:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your name Carolyn McCool?

utterances.speaker: CAROLYN McCOOL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Their Honours have your curriculum vitae. It is clear that there was a time when you had an intimate involvement in events in Kosovo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAROLYN McCOOL
utterances.text: I was in Kosovo from August 1999 until September of 2002.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see from your -- the curriculum vitae I've mentioned that you're a qualified lawyer. You've held a large number of different positions both for government and non-government agencies over a number of years. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAROLYN McCOOL
utterances.text: Yes. I was called to the bar in the province of British Columbia in Canada in 1977 and practiced law in that province until I went to Kosovo in 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we can see on the first page of the CV itself the dates you've mentioned. You were a director of the mission in Kosovo of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, the OSCE, which had at that time responsibility for supporting the development of institutions of government and civil society in line with the principles of the rule of law.

utterances.speaker: CAROLYN McCOOL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It had that mandate under UN Security Council Resolution Number 1244, I believe, if memory serves me correctly, and was the -- one of the four pillars of the United Nations Mission in Kosovo with the responsibility for what is called institution-building, and I was a director of that mission in two different capacities from 1999 until 2002.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, just linking it with Kosovo, it's clear on the third page of your CV that in June 2004 you were awarded the Canadian peacekeeping medal for service in the cause of peace in Kosovo during those years?

utterances.speaker: CAROLYN McCOOL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just briefly before we return to Kosovo, again it's on the first page of your CV, you've done a number of things since being in Kosovo. Most recently, from August to December 2004, you were commissioned by another international government organisation on constitution building in Afghanistan. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAROLYN McCOOL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I -- if I understand correctly the reference that you're making to that page of the CV, I was asked to co-author a paper on constitution building in Afghanistan by an organisation which is based in Sweden called the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: IDEA.

utterances.speaker: CAROLYN McCOOL
utterances.text: IDEA. International IDEA. And we almost never use anything but the acronym, so I was struggling with the full name. Yes, along with a young Afghan-American colleague wrote a paper on International IDEA in Stockholm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I pause so -- for the interpreters because it's being translated. I think the A is assistance in IDEA.

utterances.speaker: CAROLYN McCOOL
utterances.text: I think you're correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in January of 2005 you were drafting another paper for the establishment of an appeals commission in connection with electoral matters, again in Afghanistan?

utterances.speaker: CAROLYN McCOOL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can I take you back to Kosovo. I want to ask you about Fatmir Limaj. Do you remember when you first met him and where you first met him?

utterances.speaker: CAROLYN McCOOL
utterances.text: I've been trying to remember, anticipating that you would ask me that. I believe that the first time I met Mr. Limaj was early in 2001 at a reception that was hosted by the American embassy or the USAID for someone who was leaving or arriving. I don't remember the exact circumstances, but it was at a restaurant in Pristina, and I believe that was the first time that we met, although I'm not 100 per cent certain but I'm almost 100 per cent certain that that was the first time we ever met each other. I was the newly appointed as the director of democratisation in Pristina. Up to that point in time I had been living in Mitrovica, in the north of Kosovo and Mr. Limaj had been -- was in Pristina, so we had not known each other prior to my having gone to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall at that time what his position was?

utterances.speaker: CAROLYN McCOOL
utterances.text: Well, I think of Mr. Limaj being a vice-president of the political party, the PDK, the Democratic Party of Kosovo. And he later, after being Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. elected to the central assembly of Kosovo, became the head of the parliamentary group for the PDK in that assembly, if I remember correctly. Now, whether he held that first position of vice-president early in 2001, I can't confirm absolutely, but I believe that is so. He was a very senior member of the PDK from as far back as I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, having met him early in 2001, thereafter did you have regular contact with him?

utterances.speaker: CAROLYN McCOOL
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In a variety of different ways, which included meetings in his offices, meetings in my offices. Between the two of us alone as well as in the context of larger meetings between Albanians and Serbs and representatives of different ethnic communities in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get to know him well?

utterances.speaker: CAROLYN McCOOL
utterances.text: I think so. We -- Mr. Limaj became one of those leaders in Kosovo whom I trusted implicitly. We would talk about politics in ways which I found it very difficult to talk to a lot of people, in a way that was open and candid in which he would disclose the difficulties that he had as a leader. I would talk about the difficulties that I had as a foreigner. And it was really in the course of developing that relationship, if I may call it that, that I came to learn some of the things I didn't know I didn't know about Kosovo. And I think Mr. Limaj may have come to realise some of the things he didn't know about institution-building. So it was very much a mutual relationship in which I think we I think learned from each other, and I found it a source of -- it helped to increase my confidence level in Kosovo enormously because of the manner in which he spoke to me and the trust which I placed in his judgement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as that relationship developed, can you just describe how he approached the problems that you both were facing in that year and thereafter?

utterances.speaker: CAROLYN McCOOL
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj approached these problems which were enormous and remained enormous. The whole question of the development of a multi-ethnic society in Kosovo is one which is moving very slowly, very slowly, in its resolution. Mr. Limaj's approach, more and more, as I knew him, was to try to resolve that -- those problems, that host of problems, by talking to people. And by that, I don't simply mean foreigners like me. I mean by talking with representatives of other ethnic communities, most notably the Kosovo-Serbian community. And of course it's the relationship between the Albanian and the Serbian people which is at the heart of the history of Kosovo since at least the 1980s. Mr. Limaj, in my view, and in the period I knew him developed qualities of leadership, which included a vision of a multi-ethnic Kosovo. And he did this not simply by sitting in his office and talking to his PDK colleagues, but by leaving those offices and talking with Serbs as well as representatives of other ethnic communities, as well as foreigners such as myself. So he was one of those people that Serbian leaders were prepared to talk to and he was prepared to talk to them. This was in the context of sometimes rather public meetings, meetings that the media had been advised of and would report on later, as well as more private meetings, sometimes involving just a very few number of people which were not publicly known at all. Because one of the things that Mr. Limaj was having to do as he grew in stature as a leader was balance his vision of a developing multi-ethnic society against some of the views of some of his constituents which were still locked in the sort of historical embrace of antipathy, indeed hatred, at some levels. And he was indeed moving beyond that and prepared to talk to people about how they were going to make this thing work in the end. And this was, in my view, one of the things that was most interesting about Mr. Limaj, is that this was not done simply for the benefit of the donor community, in order to get the funding or the benefits that go with pleasing the donors in a post-conflict situation. One of the reasons that I felt continually interested in talking with him was because it was clear that he was doing this because he was developing a vision of Kosovo for the future which would serve all of the people of that land.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I appreciate it's sometimes difficult looking back to remember particular examples or events that you recognise at the time and then they're flooded out by events that happened. But are there any particular examples or events that address the issues you've just ...

utterances.speaker: CAROLYN McCOOL
utterances.text: Well, yes. There -- there were a series of -- there are a couple of ways in which I can answer that question. There were a series of meetings that were held at our offices at the OSCE, which included representatives of all ethnic communities and of course predominantly the Albanian and the Serbian people of Kosovo. Mr. Limaj was regularly one of the Albanian representatives in these meetings and regularly spoke at these meetings in a very impassioned manner. He has a -- almost a charismatic way of speaking at times. And he -- I can remember him sitting across the table in our boardroom from Serbian leaders and speaking with vehement passion about the position of the Albanian people in Kosovo, while at the same time proposing a path forward which would allow them all to get to a better future. He, in these meetings, was one of the -- regularly one of the most articulate people present without any -- without any question whatsoever. But there were also smaller meetings which Mr. Limaj agreed to be involved in with Serbian leaders at which more candid discussions took place. And I remember one meeting at which Mr. Limaj in fact proposed a whole plan of action whereby the assembly of Kosovo could engage in dialogue with similar bodies in surrounding countries and jurisdictions - with other parliamentarians basically - to work on -- he mentioned economic development as being the greatest priority on a regional basis, as well as other issues of mutual concern. And he and these Serbian leaders were in fact in agreement on this kind of plan of action. This was -- this was in the -- this was just before I left Kosovo in September of 2002. And indeed, had not Mr. Limaj come to be here, I believe that he probably would have pursued those plans. And it may be that in the end something comes of that; we shall see. So there were two ways -- in terms of actual examples, there are, again, the two types of meetings that come to my mind which I've just described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one further question on that. At any time during the occasions that you met or on any other occasion, did you ever hear him, that is Fatmir Limaj, express any derogatory or discriminatory remark about ethnic minorities, and in particular Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CAROLYN McCOOL
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, finally this: You've expressed views very clearly this afternoon. Were the views that you've expressed shared by those with whom you worked, and in particular the head of the task force, Dan Everts?

utterances.speaker: CAROLYN McCOOL
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the interpreters to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: CAROLYN McCOOL
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Limaj was widely regarded very, very well by the senior members of my mission, and that includes the man who was my head of mission for most of my time there, Dan Everts, who is from the Netherlands and I believe is working here in The Hague at some point -- or at some place these days. But Mr. Everts had a very favourable view of Mr. Limaj, as did other members of the senior management team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wonder as a postscript of that if we might exhibit as annex 5 -- it was originally annex 5. It is a letter from Dan Everts dated in 2003. It's a letter which has already been before the Tribunal on an earlier occasion and which -- part of which I read to Your Honours in the opening, and the CV, yes, if they could be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, they'll be received -- together, I think, Mr. Mansfield?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you just wait there.

utterances.speaker: CAROLYN McCOOL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The court officer needs a copy, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I think they have them but we'll provide another one now. Thank you very much. Could we submit the CV a bit later; we haven't got a spare of that at the moment. So it's just the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have a copy of the CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Oh, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This paper is tendered into exhibit under the reference DL14, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Nor I, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mrs. McCool, you'll be pleased and relieved. You're familiar enough with the procedure to realise that that concludes your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May we thank you very much for your attendance and assistance. It's been quite a long journey by the look, and we are happy to tell you that you may now of course go back to your home and your own affairs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's been my honour and a pleasure to appear in front of you today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't know whether it will speed up the process or not, but the next witness, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I'm hoping this is the witness who is now behind the door again. It's Elmi Sopi, please. Prosecution Exhibit 1 will be needed for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can I just inquire before we begin, are we going to have two directs? Is that the plan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This witness is called by two of the accused; that is my expectation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We had thought that Mr. Mansfield would do a direct, I would do a cross, Mr. Topolski would do a cross, then I would do a direct and Mr. Mansfield will do a cross. We don't want to load him up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that could be a very sound procedure, but perhaps in the interests of time we might limit you and Mr. Mansfield to one examination-in-chief each.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is put before you. Are you able to understand what is being said in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Mansfield:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sopi. I'm standing over here, representing Fatmir Limaj.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Speak slowly because, as you will appreciate, everything has to be interpreted and then I wait for the interpreter to finish before I continue. And it would be helpful if you could do the same. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your name is Elmi Sopi?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't be worried. They're not imposing anything on you. And if I may just lead you on your date of birth. You were born in the year of 1955?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And throughout your early life in Lapusnik, did you live in the same house all the time?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes. I have lived all the time in one house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: The primary school in Lapusnik and then in the high school technical school in Drenoc. I did four years of high school in Komorane and then a technical school in Drenoc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after qualifying at school, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I did the military service in Sarajevo [realtime transcript read in error "Carraleve"]. After finishing the military service, I went to Croatia to work in the construction business. And in 1979 I started to work in Ramiz Sadiku construction enterprise in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in Pristina, working in Pristina at that job?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I worked until 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: In 1992, the Belgrade regime dismissed us. We were over 8.000 workers. In that enterprise, there were about 10.000 workers. 8.000 were dismissed immediately. But this was a misfortune that befell not only to the place of work where I worked. That was something that happened to all the work establishments in Kosova, in education, in health, and in all the other organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I was alerted to an error I believe in the transcript. I think the witness said he did his military service in Sarajevo. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you had been made redundant by the Serbian government, what did you then do?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I worked with my brothers and sons in private enterprises in Kosova until the war broke out mostly in construction work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you questions which concern your personal position by the beginning of 1998. First -- sorry. First question is: Where were you living in Kosovo at the beginning of 1998?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I lived in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many other members of your family lived in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they all dotted around in different places in Lapusnik or were they concentrated in one area of Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: They were concentrated in one area. We were six brothers, and we lived in a compound, family compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I were to show you an aerial photograph of Lapusnik, would you be able to show us on the photograph where that house or compound was where you lived with your brothers?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a clean copy. It is in fact image 8 of P1, aerial image of Lapusnik. I wonder if it could be put on the monitor again, the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you very kindly just familiarise yourself with the photograph, and then I'm going to ask if you could take a felt pen and circle the place where your house was, if you can see it.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: It's here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Could you just put a circle around it so we can see.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you could -- because there may be other places we're going to ring on this photograph, could you put very obviously the number 1 against that circle.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just to be as precise as possible, by the beginning of 1998 how many of you were living in the family compound within that circle you've just put on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I think I told you earlier we were 35 members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all 35 were in the compound?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other relatives that you had that lived elsewhere in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes, nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Roughly within what distance of the circle there?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Ferat Sopi lives -- his house is divided from us by a wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: There is Shaban Sopi, Afrim Sopi, Hajrush Sopi, Nazif Sopi. They live a little bit further. On the lower part of the circle is the house of Gani Gashi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you before we move on in 1998, by this time had you joined the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you join?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I joined the KLA after the Likoshan-Qirez-Prekaz massacres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you join?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I joined the KLA because I had two friends of mine who were friends with Ferat Shala. At that time I didn't know Ferat Shala. They talked with him and they came to me, these two friends of mine, and we organised ourselves in our own village to protect the population. Before the KLA came to Lapusnik, we organised ourselves, we organised guards to protect the village from the 28th of February, 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had anything happened before the 28th of February, 1998, that --

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Before the 28th of February, 1998, on the 25th of February, 1998, in my own house came 20 policemen, Serb policemen, with an Albanian policeman who was working with them. His name was Hajdar Mustafa [phoen]. They came to arrest one of my brothers. But the day we happened not to be at home but were working out in the fields. The father came out and talked with the policemen. They told my father that they were looking for Haradin; they wanted to arrest him. My father told them that for the moment he was not there and that he would inform him and that the policemen told him these words: If he -- if Haradin doesn't come to report tomorrow to the police station in Gllogovc, we will arrest you and your entire family. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And on the next day, I had, myself, to accompany my brother to the police station. And there, Hajdar Mustafa told me that on Saturday I had to go to Komorane, it was a market day, to meet him and to tell him in which prison they had taken my brother. I went to Komorane, but unfortunately I couldn't meet Hajdar. At 12.00 I saw him running to his car, Niva, accompanied by some Serb policemen, and I couldn't speak to him about my brother -- couldn't find out which prison my brother was. Then I went to a village in Obliq municipality to a cousin of mine, the son of my aunt, and decided to go to Lipjan prison to find out whether my brother was there. When we arrived at Lipjan checkpoint -- crossroads, the Serb police stopped us. They asked me to come out of the car. I was from Gllogovc communal assembly. They surrounded me. One of them asked questions, whereas the others started to slander me and to curse me in the way they used. They beat me but they didn't kill me. On that day I decided not to go along the asphalt road. And because of the violence used against us and the massacres perpetrated, I made up my mind to join the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to your brother?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: My brother was imprisoned. To my recollection, he did 30 days of jail and then they released him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to move to the 28th of February when you began to guard the village of Lapusnik. How many of you were involved in that?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact number, but those who were there aged 18 to 50, all of them participated in this action. Before the KLA arrived in Lapusnik, we did -- we kept guard 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of you have weapons?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: No. Maybe some of us had some hunting guns, but we didn't dare give them the arms because some of them hadn't done the military service. Only those who knew how to use the weapon, the gun, we gave these hunting guns, but we didn't have any other weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have one of these hunting guns?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of you have a uniform of any kind?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: No. At that time, nobody had uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any one of you in charge of the rest?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: No. It was a voluntary form of organisation because it was a life-and-death issue for us, and everything we did, we did it on a voluntary basis to help our families and our households.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this, as you say, is before the KLA arrived. When did the KLA arrive?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: The KLA arrived on the 9th of May in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe, please, what happened on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: On the date, on the 9th of May, Serb police forces came and took positions in Gradines Guri at about 8.00 in the morning. We were all following developments. They went to Gradines Guri above the school. Without any pretexts, without any reason, they started to fire at the entire village, all over the place. I went and took my sick father, my grandmother, who was over 90, and my mother, and took out my car and we couldn't move because the war -- the roads were unpassable, blocked. There was a helicopter of the Serb forces that was flying above my car. I asked my father, grandmother, and my mother to come out of the car and I hid them in the forest and myself took refuge there until the helicopter flew away. And then at around 11.00 Ymer Alushani came with seven or eight comrades. All of them were dressed in civilian clothes, but all of them were armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that day, did you know Ymer Alushani?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I knew him since childhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he live in Lapusnik or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: No. He lives in Komorane -- he has lived in Komorane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when they -- when he came with seven or eight comrades, what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I told Ymer what was happening. He came and asked me what was happening after having heard the shots. I told him of the situation and showed him where the Serb police forces were deployed. I also showed him where some youths from the village were, some of them who had hunting guns. And I told Ymer to go to the house of Haxhi Gashi or Kadri because there you can find these youths. I couldn't leave alone my parents and grandmother. Ymer went to this house and met these people. After one hour, I saw another group of soldiers descending from the mountains. They were about 16 persons, all of them were armed. Two or three or four were dressed in military clothes, in uniform. I called my brother, Valdet, and I told him to go and join this group that was sheltered at Haxhiu's house. And the two groups got together there, and my brother, Valdet, and Ramiz Sopi led these people to go to the place where the Serbs were stationed because they didn't know Lapusnik, the terrain, and didn't know which was the best place to come closer to the Serb forces. At about 13 hours, I heard the fire. I was far away but I saw a smoke, a black smoke, rising. I left my parents and grandmother and went to another place to have a better look. I saw the Serb forces withdrawing towards Komorane. Then I went to see what had happened on the site of the fighting. I saw a Pinzgauer were in flames. It was a Serb police Pinzgauer. And I saw munitions -- numerous arms and munitions -- no, the Pinzgauer had a lot of munitions and it was all in flames. For a long time we didn't dare go near the place because of explosives -- because of explosions. Correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned there that a second group of 16 descended from the mountains. Did you know any of the 16 that you saw?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: No, I didn't know any one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this day, that is the 9th of May, 1998, please describe how events evolved over the next few days and weeks in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: After 9th of May --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, after the 9th of May, sorry.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, we have an action and the Serbian forces were expelled. We, the villagers, remained alone because those who helped us who wanted to go where they came from. We knew Ymer Alushan and asked him not to leave us on the fate's sake, on the mercy of the fates and to help us further and to look for the possibility to house us. We asked him [indiscernible]. We can house him and can settle him and for all his soldiers, only don't leave us alone. Ymer Alushan discussed that with his friends, and it's for sure that he discussed that with the other group which -- starting from 19th of May were placed in our houses -- 9th of May, excuse me. At the beginning there were only a few of them and we as villagers helped them a lot and to position themselves and to have munitions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you, yourself, do in those days and weeks after the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I engaged myself into helping the friends in digging up trenches, in organising -- in better organisation in order to protect the population because we were on the first front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any way you can help by looking at the aerial photograph again, which is to your left. Would it be possible on that photograph just to point out the trenches that you've mentioned you were digging?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could do it with a felt -- if you wouldn't mind doing it with a felt pen, just circling the area where you were digging the trenches and putting a 2, a number 2, next to it.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Here is the Lapusnik school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just -- we're not quite on screen. Just pause one minute. Right. It's now on screen. Can you just point to the school again. You've just mentioned it. Can you point to it.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Here on this spot below the Pristina-Peja main road is the Lapusnik school. Here on the 9th of May were the Serb positions. They were positioned here at this guri or rock. Shall I mark it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. If you wouldn't mind just doing a --

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: So here is the school and here were the Serb forces. Here -- the mountain shows a place where the Pinzgauer was burnt down. We established some positions above the place where the Pinzgauer was. Shall I mark the line where the positions were?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Could you -- before you mark the line where the positions were, could you just give a number to the circle you've just done where the school and so on -- put a number 2 by that so we can keep up with it. If you could put a number 2.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Mark the school 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Serb positions with 3.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then with a line mark where you were digging trenches after that.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Starting from here there was a canal, a position, and it ran along this line. This line was a trench where the positions were. Here there was a sheltering place on the corner, and here is the road, up to this field here. And here it continued again, the line of positions. There were no positions here. And here there was some positions. And these positions are along this road. Here the position enters the opposite side of the road and continues like this. There was another trench that continued along this line and up to this place. These are the positions that existed at Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Would you just concentrate on this for a moment. It's plain that trenches as extensive as that cannot have been made overnight. Can you help us as to when these trenches were dug and the order in which they were dug?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: There was no trench on the 9th of May. From 9th of May onwards, every day we dug up canals. The canal here, we opened it here. After three or four days, the other one, because every day there was constant firing, shooting, and there was no place for us to shelter. In addition, this road here at the gas station, Thaqi brothers, the road that goes down here, we opened another position here in case the Serb forces came and entered the village. These two positions were on the first day -- well, not on the first day but they were there after seven or eight days. Then for some time, the youths from the village engaged in this. And as a number of soldiers grew in Lapusnik, the trenches were then extended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By what time do you think that the exercise of building trenches that you have described had finished? Are we still in May; the next month, June; or even July?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: No. This took us, if I can say, to the very fall of the gorge. This was done in June and July and everyone, like, worked on his own, open trenches on his own. But facing the risk then, we opened the positions in order to be able to withdraw. So it took us up to the time when the gorge fell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we know the date of that, which was the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this any other fighting between the 9th of May and the 26th of July in which you were involved?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes. I will say this: As of 9th of May there were many fightings; however, the most severe one was the fighting of the 29th of May. The combat went on for 16 hours. There were fightings before this date as well, but they were of insignificant intensity, in which the Serb police forces always used the weekends for these attacks because those few humanitarian organisations, international organisations, operating in Kosova were on holidays during weekends. And Serb police forces took advantage of this so that they wouldn't be seen by the international community in their deeds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we come to the 29th of May, by that date did you have a radio that you could use?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge whether there was radio or not. I didn't see anybody communicating via radio, and therefore I cannot say that there was one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the 29th of May, did you have a uniform?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Not more than seven, eight, or ten persons had uniforms. Some made their uniforms out of the material of some military tents. Otherwise there were no uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the members of the KLA you were serving alongside, did the group have a name or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Well, as of the second day I found out that the unit was called Celiku 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom did you find that out?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I was told by Ymer Alushani about this because I didn't know the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during this period, were orders or commands being given to each of you, and in particular obviously yourself?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: No. I didn't receive any orders because in the beginning we were organised as villagers. Later on, they came and whoever came to Lapusnik to protect the population was holy to us because we didn't go to wage a war in Belgrade, but they came to our thresholds. And that's why I'm saying that they were holy, sacred, to us for the help they provided us with, for preventing the Serbs from committing massacres over the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so far as weapons are concerned, were you still using your hunting rifle or did you have other weapons by then, that's by the 29th of May?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Some had Kalashnikovs, some had M-48, some had old weapons which names I don't know, but mostly we had hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What proportion of the people around you knew how to use the weapons, were trained in using the weapons?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: No. Most of them had not completed their military service, as I said earlier. Even us as villagers, when we stood guard duty, many who didn't know how to use a weapon were not given one. At positions, they learned from each other, the one who had knowledge of how to operate a weapon taught the other, and that's how all of us came to learn how to use a weapon and to fulfil our duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, may I return to the 29th of May. Can you just describe what happened on that day, please.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I can tell you that fighting began at 7.00 in the morning, to my recollection, on the 29th of May, and they went on until 9.00 or 10.00 p.m. On that day, many soldiers from different areas came to assist us. I didn't know them, but on that time -- day, I saw Fatmir Limaj as well as he came to assist us together with Kumanova, who is Ismet Jashari. There was also Haradin Bala. When I heard Kumanova asking him, Why are you not here? You should come with me. Because Haradin Bala was of poor health.
