I don't have any knowledge whether they knew each other, Kumanova and Haradin, but this is what he told him. And after the 29th of May, Haradin -- I no longer saw Haradin at Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Fatmir Limaj. Had you seen him in Lapusnik before the 29th of May?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him during the first fightings on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had you ever met him before that, namely before the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: No, never. I didn't know him, I didn't know who he was and where he was from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as you're aware, did Fatmir Limaj ever give you or anyone else that you were aware of any orders or commands?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear Fatmir Limaj giving order or command to someone because he rarely came to Lapusnik. And on the occasions I saw him, he did not come to Lapusnik to give orders but he came to fight. I always saw him at the positions and in my courtyard and in my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during -- you mentioned obviously your house which you've ringed. I want to ask you about a particular building. Did the -- did your group of soldiers have a kitchen at any time which you used?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: After the 9th of May for five or six days they brought us food from Komorane, the villagers of Komorane brought us food. After five or six days, we began to organise ourselves and we had our kitchen in the house of Fadil Gashi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It may not be possible, but looking at the aerial photograph again can we see his house on that, where the kitchen was situated?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I will continue for a bit more. The kitchen at Fadil Gashi's house, we had it until the 29th of May. Shall I mark it, Fadil Gashi's house?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please, with another circle. And I think we're up to number 4.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: [Marks]. If I may continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: In this house was the kitchen, as I said, five or six days after 9th of May and until the 29th of May. On the 29th of May, as I mentioned earlier, the combat went on for 16 hours. We went there to the kitchen to have dinner. When we gathered, let's say we were about 50 soldiers except for the guards who were on their positions, all of us were there in the kitchen. The Serb forces from the field shelled us. And as of 29th of May, we could no longer stay in this house because of the shelling and also in the houses near the positions that I marked earlier, and therefore went to the house of Gzim Gashi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, still looking at the aerial photograph, can you indicate where the house of Gzim is?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Shall I mark it with 5?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before the kitchen -- kitchen moved from position number 4 to position number 5, during these months, May, -- April/May of 1998, had you occasion to go into the vicinity of the house at number 5?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question. Did you say before April and May?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, it's my fault. It is in fact during April and May, did you have occasion, were there times when you went to that part of Lapusnik near Gzim's house where the kitchen eventually came?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Again, it's not clear to me, April and May when you say, because before May there wasn't a kitchen there. I went to his house because he's a neighbour of mine; he's only 200 metres away from my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. No, you've answered the question. How often did you go to his house because he's a neighbour during April and May of 1998, before the kitchen got there and before the 29th?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I went there because the owner of the house and my father are relatives; their mothers are first cousins. And I have family relations with him; he is my neighbour and a relative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. Can I just ask you again. About how often would you go? I mean, once a week? Every other week?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I can tell you that from May until the end of July I went maybe 15 times. As for the kitchen, I went there every day to have my meal. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time. I'm trying to work out where we should be at. I think probably this is the right time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's within the right range, Mr. Mansfield. We will resume at 25 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sopi, I think it was entirely my fault that the questions just before the break might have been confusing. So I just want, if I may, to repeat them more clearly. I'm dealing with your visits to the house at number 5 on the photograph, Gzim Gashi's house, and I will split up the time period. Firstly, in March and April of 1998, how often do you think you went to his house?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: To my recollection, I went three to four times during March and April 1998. I spoke with his sons. Only one of his sons is in his house. And we discussed the issue of organising guard duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in the period -- and I'll take it just May for the moment. In the period of May, the month of May, how often do you think you went to the same house?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Are you referring to Gzim Gashi's house?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: These two or three times that I mentioned I didn't go very often. I went to Shajip's [phoen] house more often because he was there in his house at all times, while Gzim did not stay in his house. He's a young man; he went out often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, may we just move on to the time after the 29th of May. Can you describe what was happening on a daily basis from the end of May through June and into July?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: After the 29th of May, the kitchen was set up as Gzim's house where almost all the soldiers had their meals, in his house. I, as well, had my meals with them. Sometimes I didn't go there because I had my house in the village, so I didn't go to have dinner in the kitchen. However, soldiers who did not have houses at Lapusnik, they went three times a day to have their meals at his house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the day in this period, that's after the 29th of May, can you just describe generally what you were doing. Were you digging ditches, standing on guard? What sort of things were you doing?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: From 9th of May onwards, every day soldiers who were free would take the weapons and stay in their positions. They would dig up the trenches and they were helped in this work by the population, by the youth from the village who were able to perform physical work. I would like to explain you one thing. These positions that I marked here with a line were built mostly at nighttime and not during the day because you were not able to make any movement during the day because of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to move to a time towards the 26th of July. Did you -- did there come a time when you changed units?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes. In the end of June, I, as I mentioned in the beginning, had my friends with me, Jahir and Muhamed. There were in the Pellumbi unit and I saw it reasonable for me to go to this unit. As the 25th and 26th July approached, I was in the Pellumbi unit. However, I would like to point out that I stood guard duty and had agreed with my friends who were standing guard duty in Celiku 3 unit. After completing my task at the position, every day to go and sleep in my own house, whether it was during the day or at night, depending on my shift. My house was only one kilometre or one and a half kilometres away from the positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was the decision to move to the Pellumbi 1 one that you took yourself or were you told to change? How did it work?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: No. I decided myself because I had my brothers who were helping the KLA. Therefore, I decided on my own without asking anyone because I had my personal weapon. Nobody gave me this weapon. It was mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would you kindly look at the aerial photograph again. And if it's possible on that same photograph, could you indicate where the Pellumbi unit you joined was based.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: In this part --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we move it --

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: It's not shown here --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps we could --

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: -- the place where Pellumbi was. But I can describe it in words. As you see this road here, the gas station, there are some houses here. I will make a mark with my pen outside the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you number that number 6, please.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: These were positions of Pellumbi unit; they were here. Along the Pristina-Peja main road in the direction of Peja, when going towards Peja, they were on the right side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Guri unit -- I'm so sorry. Did the Pellumbi unit have a number?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I know for Guri 3, but I don't remember whether Pellumbi had a number. I know it as Pellumbi unit only. Whether there were two -- there was number 2 or number 3, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone in charge of the Pellumbi unit you joined?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes. Commander of the Pellumbi unit was Ferat Shala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just while we're dealing with it, can you show us on this aerial photograph where the unit called Guri 3 was?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: The place where Guri 3 operated, shall I mark it with number 7?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: It's here, but another part of Guri 3 unit was in one part of Lapusnik, that part that is attached to Krajkove village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it that's not on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can I return to the events of July the 26th. Where were you on that day?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I was where I marked number 6; I was in this place. These were the Pellumbi positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were your family at that time?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: One part of my family who were not able to flee, they remained in the house, but not the entire family. Some were in Berisa and some in Fshati i Ri or Novoselle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened on that day, 26th of July?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: On the 26th of July, I was in my house. I completed my guard duty with the Pellumbi unit, returned home. And on the 26th of July, at 4.00 a.m., my friends called me and told me from Komri i Britit [phoen] location the main road Pristina-Peja, they had seen a convoy of Serb tanks and machinery moving towards Komorane. In Komorane, there was a checkpoint before the 28th of February. They stopped there for some time, and the tanks that were positioned at Quka e Komoranit and the Serb machinery positioned at the radio Pristina antenna in Komorane and the chicken farm in Krajkove, they all set off towards the Lapusnik gorge time. Sometime in the morning the shooting started from all directions. They were firing at us with Kaquqas [phoen] from the pine trees in Krajkove with cannons of 220 millimetre from Golesh. And I can say that more than 140 tanks were engaged in combat against KLA members at the Lapusnik gorge, let alone APCs and Pragas, and other equipment with which names I'm not familiar with. This was on the 25th of July, which was Saturday. On the 26th of July, we were not able to confront them and began to withdraw from the positions. This was the most difficult offensive for us throughout the war. The entire population moved from the Lapusnik gorge to Negrovce, Orlate, Terpeze, and climbed up the mountains wherever they could go. They had no food, no clothes, no conditions for life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have at that time any weapons at all that could deal with tanks and APCs, armoured personnel carriers, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: No, we didn't have those. We had some mortars, 150-millimetre ones. And even if you shot at a tank or an APC with them, you could cause no damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on this same day, that's the 26th of July, did you hear some personal tragic news?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I didn't hear any news on the 26th of July, but I did hear news on the 27th. I was informed by the martyr to the nation, Fehmi Lladrovci; I met him at Negrovce village. I asked him about part of Celiku unit. He told me that Ymer Alushani fell heroically and that Ali Zogi and Fetah Zogu were injured. He had heard that my wife died on that day in Novoselle village because of fear, but he didn't tell me that because the circumstances were such that it was difficult to go to that part of Berisa Mountains since the Pristina-Peja main road had a tank positioned on it at every 50 metres. Even on the Malisheve road they had positioned such equipments because they had plenty of military equipment. This is the reason why Fehmi didn't tell me about the death of my wife. After five or six days, I went out with some friends of mine. I started my journey at 1.00 p.m. and arrived at Berisa Mountains at 5.00 in the morning. A road that someone can make just in one hour or one hour and a half, however it took me this long because of the Serb forces. I went to Berisa, met a villager there, and he paid his condolences to me, knowing what had happened. When he realised that I was not aware of my wife's death, he said that he was mistaken, but I insisted that he told me what had happened. And he said that out of fear she died because she thought myself and my son got killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned your son. Where was he serving as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: He served at Celiku 3 unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you this question: Are you aware of how many Lapusnik villagers died at the hands of the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell you that from the beginning of the war and until the end, 33 civilians and soldiers killed by the Serb forces in the village of Lapusnik. There were also mentally -- there was also a mentally ill person who was killed and thrown in a well just to lose traces of his body. In addition, bodies of elderly persons were burnt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there came a time when you were able to return to the Lapusnik village, and I believe you were one of the first villagers to return. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What had happened to your house meanwhile?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Together with some comrades, soldiers, I came down from the Berisa Mountains and settled at the positions where the positions -- the Serbs were positioned until one hour ago near my house. We checked for mines just to prevent the population from a disaster. I went to the garden which is above my house, and there I found five hand-grenades. The fuses were ready to ignite. I removed them, the mines, and then I went first to my home, then I went to all the other houses of the village to see whether the Serbs had left behind mines or some other explosives. But we didn't find any, with exception of the hand-grenades I mentioned earlier. We didn't find anything. In the three neighbourhoods we went, Salihaj, Sopi, and Guri, we didn't see any mines, but the houses were destroyed; people couldn't live there. I returned to a cowshed we had, and our 35 members slept there at that cowshed until I received some assistance and started to build the roof of my home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us roughly when it was that you returned to your house and found what you've just described?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: On the 13th of June, the Serb forces left the village, and that is the last force -- Serb forces had left the village at Gradina rock. When I went there, as I said earlier, to my house, the Serb forces were still at Gradina rock, and this happened on the 13th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it goes without saying, you left the year out, but it's 1999 that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes, it is 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I have one final question for you. During 1998 whilst you were still living in Lapusnik in May, June, and July, did you hear of a prison in the village?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I'm telling you the truth that it was only after the arrest of my friends that I heard that, and not only myself personally but the entire village were taken by surprise at that news because we've never heard about that, we've never seen anything during that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Would you wait there, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mansfield. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Examined by Mr. Guy-Smith:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sopi.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I represent Haradin Bala. Do you know Haradin Bala?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes. I have known him since we were children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how is it you've known him since you were children?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Haradin Bala is a nephew in Lapusnik. In addition to that, we went to the primary school in Komorane together. And to complete the picture, I want to tell you that his father was a close friend with a brother of my mother, so I knew him pretty well. I knew his families well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It certainly sounds as if you do. Could you tell us, please, since you mentioned his father whether or not his father had any special skills during the time that he was alive?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: His father was a singer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say that his father was a singer, did he sing privately or publicly, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: He sang publicly at weddings. He was a rhapsodic singer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Haradin a rhapsodic singer also? Did he inherit that quality from his father?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: No, I don't think Haradin can sing like his father. He can never resemble his father for that matter in that respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned that Haradin was a nephew of Lapusnik. Can you explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I think I mentioned earlier that his uncles live at the gas station some 50 metres away, and I've seen him visiting his uncles. And in the school we went together. His mother was born in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say his uncles were at the gas station, which uncles is that or were those?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Ali Thaqi; his father his called Hajdin. There is Afrim Thaqi. I don't want to mention all of them now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You also, when speaking earlier, mentioned a gentleman by the name of Ferat Sopi. Who is he?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: He is my cousin, my -- our fathers have their father's brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he still alive?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is he working? And if he is, could you tell us what he does for a profession.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: No, he doesn't work. He used to be a pharmacist. I wanted to say something more about that. We have lived in the same compound with him until 1969 or 1970. We lived in the same house. And he worked, as far as I know, from -- until the beginning of the war in Gllogovc in the public health house there. After the war, he is retired. He gets 40 euros as a pension and sits at home. But he had another house in Prizren, and for the moment he lives there with his wife and a son. His two other sons live in Lapusnik. One is in England, I think, somewhere, and I think three or four days ago he went to -- he travelled to England -- or to Canada I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said that he was a pharmacist, directing your attention to the years 1990, if you know, was he a pharmacist working in Lapusnik at that time?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: He was working in the state outpatient clinic. It was called the public health house in Drenoc. But he also had a pharmacy in his own home -- house which is 10 metres away from the main road. There is another house of his. There he had a pharmacy, a drugstore, which belonged to Mother Teresa but he worked there. In his own home was this pharmacy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Mother Teresa clinic that he worked with, do you know if there was a doctor who also worked at that clinic? And by that -- this would be in the period of 1998.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Before the 9th of May, Ferat, when I mentioned that pharmacy he had, he had it in the other house. But before the 9th of May, he -- he transferred all the medicaments he had in that Mother Teresa pharmacy and brought them to the house -- his other house near my house in Lapusnik. Before the 9th of May -- I'm telling you this because I don't remember the date very well, but when I said earlier that we used to observe, to survey the terrain, fearing the coming of the Serb forces, after what happened in Likoshan, Qirez, and Prekaz, we kept on duty as I told 24 hours for 24 hours. And one day, I think it was four or five days before the 9th of May, the Serb police forces brought a dead body, a corpse, on the road that leads to Salihaj, Sopi, and Guri neighbourhoods in the evening it was, and they placed it there. The population of Lapusnik was displaced on that day because we thought that the Serb brought that corpse in order to have a pretext to act, as they did in Likoshan, Qirez and Prekaz. For the same reason, Ferat moved his pharmacy from that lower place to the other house near my house. And when you asked me the question whether the doctor Zeqe Gashi came there and helped him, the population -- that catered for the needs of the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that Dr. Zec Gashi came and helped him and the population in Lapusnik, do you remember as you sit here today whether that occurred before May 9th or after May 9th?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: This happened after the 9th of May; that was when Zeqe came, but I don't remember the date and I don't want to give you a wrong date. And I think that was not very important for us to remember when Zeqe came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Could you help us here a bit, and this is important and if you can that would be quite good; if you can't it's understandable. Do you remember whether or not Dr. Gashi came to help Ferat and the population of Lapusnik before the battle of the -- May 29th that you've discussed with here today or after that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I have -- if I may, just two points, Your Honour. One, the witness says he doesn't remember and he doesn't want to speculate. And second, I would point out that there's not one word about this issue in the 65 ter summary. And we've discussed this actual 65 ter, counsel and myself. There been no notice whatsoever that this issue was going to be brought up in the direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He's correct that it's not in the 65 ter summary and it's something that actually came to mind as a result of a document I received yesterday from the Prosecution in which there was a discussion specifically concerning assertions made by L-64 to the Prosecution on the 26th of May of this year in which that particular witness had discussion concerning Dr. Gashi and Ferat Sopi's home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And it is -- excuse me. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what's coming, but maybe it should not be in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And it's because of my receipt of this belated information that this issue came to my mind because in fact it raises the issue of Ferat Sopi and others who may have been about him and his home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's clearly relevant, Mr. Guy-Smith. You may proceed. But if there is significance in the issue and it produces difficulty for the Prosecution because of lack of notice, there may be time delay consequences. But that's something we can't immediately foresee.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand -- I understand the concern of the Chamber. And if there are any time delay issues that arise, I apologise before they do. However, I will keep this short, and I believe the issue will be both well crystallised as well as well ventilated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I just say, Your Honour, that the disclosure may have refreshed his memory as to the issue, but this issue was alive and existed well before the other disclosure had been referred to in other disclosures and I believe in another 65 ter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To that extent, I thank the Prosecution for assisting my feeble mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sopi, do you have my question in mind or should I ask it again, because there's been a fair bit of conversation since I asked the question.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I remember when you said that Zeqe said -- you asked me whether the clinic was open prior to or after the 29th of May. I'm telling you that it's a long time since then, and I don't remember the exact date. I don't remember whether it was the 29th, or the 12th, or the 15th. I cannot tell you this because I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to where the clinic was, was that clinic at Ferat Sopi's home, next to your house, or was it somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: It was next to my house, in Ferat Sopi's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that in the area that you have circled and marked with a number 1 on Prosecution 1, image 8, the document that you discussed with Mr. Mansfield?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes. Five -- it is five or six metres far from my house. Now it's completely ruined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to return to a discussion of Haradin Bala. Did you have an opportunity to see Haradin Bala in Lapusnik in the month of May 1998?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes. Haradin Bala came after -- some days after the 9th of May. I don't remember the date. I personally have seen him and told Haradin, knowing that he had poor health, I told him, Why are you here? And he said these words to me. He said, The house which is about 200 metres away from the Prishtine-Peja road, he said, that house -- I cannot stay in that house. I want to come and die here like a man. And I saw there and told him that, You have ill health. I knew he was suffering from a heart condition and that at that time it was very hot during the day; at night it was cold. I saw him there. He stayed by the end of May, and I saw him in the fighting of the 29th of May. And then Haradin didn't stay in Lapusnik --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Sir, before you go any further. You say that you knew that he had poor health. Could you tell us how long you had known that he had been in poor health before him coming to Lapusnik sometimes after May 9th?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes, I may freely tell you that because when I spoke earlier I said I worked in that Ramiz Sadik enterprise. I worked as a driver. Then they dismissed me from my work and then I had a lot of free time on my hands and I met often with Haradin, both in the street, at his uncle's, in the market-place in Komorane, and I asked him about his health because I know that his father, too, had poor health and he told me that he was suffering from a heart condition. And so I knew that he wasn't feeling well. This is why I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he told you that he was suffering from a heart condition, this is -- is this information that you received before you saw him in Lapusnik after May 9th, 1998?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I knew this since 1992 because I knew that he was sick since that time. I explained to you that when they fired me from my job in Ramiz Sadiku enterprise, I met him often and knew that he was suffering from a heart condition. His brother, Hamdi, who is in Switzerland, was a good friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you saw him in the fighting on the 29th of May in 1998 in Lapusnik. My question to you is: After that time, did you see him or did you not see him in Lapusnik again during the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him in Lapusnik, with the exception of seeing him in August. From what I remember, it was either the mid or the end of August. I saw him in the new village, in Novoselle, where I met him. Haradin Bala was with a car. I talked with him. I went there to get supplies and Haradin was there. I met him there and I asked him where he was, and he replied that he was in Luzhnice and that his family was in Bajice. It was settled there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say his family was settled in Bajice, this is a family that you knew. Is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether -- you knew Haradin's family. And if I might lead --

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I know each and every one of the family members. I know his brothers, I know the sons of the brothers. I know only one son of Haradin's children, but I don't remember his name even though he showed me his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when Haradin's family moved to Bajice in the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: They were moved to Bajice village, and I told you that his wife is born in that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my question to you is: Do you know what month that occurred? Did that occur in March, April, May, June, July?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I cannot know when that happened, but I told you Haradin told me that his family is in Bajice. But as to when or at the time when he took the family to Bajice, this I don't know. But I know that he couldn't stay long. Nobody could stay in their homes along the Prishtine-Pej main road. That was nothing that mattered to me, to tell you the truth, when he moved his family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question. Do you know what village Haradin lived in before the war in the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: He lived in Korretice e Eperme, upper Korretice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a final question which is -- that was one more and this is a final question. Could you tell us, if you know, how far his village in Korretice is from Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly, but it may be five kilometres or five kilometres and a half. About five kilometres, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sopi. You may wait there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Topolski --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Powles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Powles.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Powles:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sopi. Just a few questions on behalf of Mr. Musliu, who sits behind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: May we go into private session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in public session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sopi, the person that you just mentioned, did you see him in Lapusnik during the period that you were there in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first see him in Lapusnik in that year?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: After May, after the 9th of May, some days of that date he came to Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Sopi. How many days after the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I cannot give you an exact estimate, but four or five days after that date he came to Lapusnik. I met him in my own yard and he told me -- he introduced himself to me. We talked and he showed me in my own yard how to train -- how to train the sniper weapon because he was a good sniper. He stayed there in Lapusnik for a time --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pause there please, Mr. Sopi. During the period that he stayed in Lapusnik, how often did you see him?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how often during a day would you see him?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Once or twice, sometimes even three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time during the period that you were in Lapusnik that you no longer saw this person in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Listen. After a while, I can't tell you how long he stayed in Lapusnik. He stayed in Lapusnik, yes. That person was -- his only weakness was he was rather independent and individualistic. He didn't like to spend time with comrades. He was polite but didn't like very much to go out with friends, to socialise. Personally, I have met him outside the positions in a place and told him, Why are you here? He said, I'm a sniper and a sniper should stay alone. He was there in the position when we had already prepared the trenches. And I envied him because he was brave. It took a lot of courage and guts to be there where he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there, Mr. Sopi. I'll ask you again. You said you saw him two, sometimes three times a day. Did there come a time during the period that you were in Lapusnik that you no longer saw him?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes. I said maybe after three weeks. I didn't see him anymore in Lapusnik. You can make your own calculations. From the 12th or the 14th of May, he stayed until the end of May, and then after that I didn't see him any longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on. Did there come -- well, let me put it this way. Towards the end of July, were you involved in any operations outside of Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes. I participated in the Rahovec fighting together with eight comrades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you go to Rahovec?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I don't recall the date but I know that it was a Saturday. Whether it was the 17th, the 18th, or the 19th of July, I don't know. I didn't have a calendar then, but I know that it was a Saturday around 4.00 in the morning and that I left Rahovec on Monday. As to the dates, I can't give you exact dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you go to Rahovec --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Sorry, Your Honours, I just want to again put on the record there's been absolutely no notice whatsoever of the testimony on the issue since Mr. Powles started. The witness appears to be testifying now for three accused, not just two, and I'm curious why we did not get a 65 ter with these topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls is as ever observant. There was no 65 ter summary in relation to this witness submitted on behalf of Mr. Musliu. He is not called as a witness by us and according -- pursuant to the Rules there is no necessity for us to submit such a 65 summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Anything further?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Just you've talked about earlier in this trial about when there is a real cross-examination and when there is a real contradiction between the witnesses between the interests of the accused, and it seems to me to be the type of evidence that we should have received some notice of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is one matter, that is whether Mr. Powles might examine or cross-examine. So far he has not brought that issue alive in the way he has questioned. There is a quite separate matter, whether he might deal with issues with a witness called by another of the accused, and that's where we are at the moment. I believe he is correct when he says there is no specific rule. It's not all together surprising because there are matters over which there is no specific rule; this is one of them. We are finding our own way. Fairness and practicality will guide the Chamber. I certainly do not propose to stop Mr. Powles at present --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I don't request that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Whether there is some consequential difficulty for you, we will see. Mr. Powles.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sopi, who did you go to Rahovec with?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I went together with eight comrades, but they belonged to Pellumbi unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you go to Rahovec?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: To assist the civilian population because we heard what was happening in Rahovec and we decided, nine of us, to go. We informed a person who was with us. We told him to tell Ferat Shala that we had left for Rahovec. We took our cars, went up to Malisheve. In Malisheve, we left the cars there. And then from Malisheve to the place. Some unknown person -- to Rahovec, some unknown persons accompanied us. They took us to Rasat e Rahovecit which is a crossroad that which leads to Xerxe and Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sopi, you mentioned you were in Rahovec from approximately 4.00 until Monday. During the time you were in Rahovec, did you see Mr. Musliu?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: First I'm telling you that my friends, my comrades, told me that they had seen Isak at the time. I didn't know him as such but as Qerqizi. They told me that they had seen Qerqizi. Then I remembered that I had met Isak Musliu at the Rahovec-Rasa crossroads, but as -- whether it was Saturday or Sunday, this I cannot tell you. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say you left Rahovec on Monday. When you left, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: It was hard to leave Rahovec because we were staying at a cold room or a cellar. It's a cellar in the middle of the city. That's where our position was. And it was hard for us to leave because we were surrounded by Serb forces. We set out towards a road that leads to Hoxhe. It's a road which now I don't know in Brestovc. We left between Brnjak and Rahovec, and we went towards Pataqen and Drenoc. And then I returned to Malisheve. From Malisheve, I returned home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "home," where do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: When I say "home," I mean my own home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is your own home or was your own home at that time?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: The home that I showed you when I marked number 1 in the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your home in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you got to Lapusnik, did you at any time see Isak Musliu or Qerqiz there?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether because as far as I know Qerqiz and Ymer Alushani were still in Rahovec because a friend of ours, a comrade, a war comrade, Enver Mulaku was his name, he remained in Rahovec. He couldn't -- he was unable to leave Rahovec. And they were searching for him. I may not know but I think I saw Isak Musliu on the 24th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... there please, Mr. Sopi. Where did you see Mr. Isak Musliu on the 24th of July?

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I met him in the courtyard of my own house. He was together with some comrades. When fighting broke out in Fushtice, they had gone there to assist in the fighting. That's where I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all --

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: And if you allow me to complete it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: ELMI SOPI
utterances.text: I knew that Ymer and Isak Musliu came and brought no news of Enver Mulaku. That's why I remember very well because I asked them what happened to Enver because Enver had disappeared at that time about 10 or 12 days. We didn't have news about him; we didn't know where he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- I forgot to ask for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Tendering of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- as an exhibit. I made a note to raise it in re-examination, but we might as well do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, DL15 I think. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Indeed this piece of exhibit marked today by the witness and representing aerial image of Lapusnik is tendered into -- admitted into evidence under DL15, 1-5. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nicholls, there were a number of matters raised then you may want time to consider.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I could do that much in ten minutes anyway, Your Honour. If it's just the same, we could start tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's whatever suits you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine. Then if we just continue in the morning -- in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of June, 2005, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24
